Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
let $\gamma_{S^2}$ be the unit round metric and $\omega_{S^2}$ its positively
oriented area form. The **dyonic RN datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

In product coordinates the $v,r$ block is
$$\begin{pmatrix}-f&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},$$
with determinant $-1$ and inverse
$$\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&f\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its eigenvalues have opposite signs because their product is negative. The
sphere block $r^2\gamma$ is positive definite for $r>0$, so $g_{\mathrm{in}}$
is a smooth nondegenerate Lorentzian metric on the stated product. The
two-form is smooth since $r^{-2}$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$ and $\omega$ is
global.

The product fields $\partial_v,\partial_r$ are global and smooth, hence
so are $\ell,n,N$. Direct contraction gives
$g(\ell,\ell)=g(n,n)=0$, $g(\ell,n)=-1$,
$g(N,N)=-2$, and $g(\ell,N)=g(n,N)=-1$. Thus $N$ is an everywhere timelike
field and fixes the asserted time orientation; [F3] then makes both nonzero
null fields $\ell,n$ future-directed.

On any component where $f\ne0$, substitute $dv=dt+f^{-1}dr$ into
$-f\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr$. The mixed terms cancel and the radial coefficient
is $f^{-1}$, giving $-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2$. Also
$dv\wedge dr=dt\wedge dr$, so $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}$ becomes the
static two-form in [F1]. The substitution is defined separately on each
component where $f\ne0$; it does not extend $r_*$ through a root.

On $f>0$, $\partial_t=\partial_v$ and
$g(\partial_v,N)=-1-f/2<0$, so the exterior orientations agree. On $f<0$,
the static-coordinate vector is
$\partial_r|_t=\partial_r|_v+f^{-1}\partial_v$, and
$g(\partial_r|_t,N)=1/2-1/f>0$; hence the static definition's
$\partial_r|_t$ is past-directed under the selected ingoing orientation.
This proves the stated convention boundary and makes no identification of
the two interior time orientations.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. $$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

derivations.claim:
Pulling [F1]'s $\mathcal F$ back to $S_r$ removes the electric term and
leaves $q_m\omega$. Since
$$\int_{S^2}\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi,$$
the first flux is $4\pi q_m$. The inverse static metric has
$g^{tt}=-1/f$, $g^{rr}=f$, and the oriented volume form is
$r^2\sin\theta\,dt\wedge dr\wedge d\theta\wedge d\phi$. In the component
formula of [F2],
$(dt\wedge dr)^{tr}=g^{tt}g^{rr}=-1$ and
$\omega^{\theta\phi}=1/(r^4\sin\theta)$. The oriented volume component is
$\epsilon_{\theta\phi tr}=r^2\sin\theta$, so that formula gives
$$\star_g(dt\wedge dr)=-r^2\omega,\qquad \star_g\omega=r^{-2}dt\wedge dr,$$
for either sign of $f$. Therefore
$\star_g\mathcal F=q_e\omega+q_m r^{-2}dt\wedge dr$; its sphere pullback
integrates to $4\pi q_e$.

On $U_N=\{r+z>0\}$ and $U_S=\{r-z>0\}$, respectively,
$$ (1-\cos\theta)d\phi=\frac{x\,dy-y\,dx}{r(r+z)},\qquad (1+\cos\theta)d\phi=\frac{x\,dy-y\,dx}{r(r-z)}.$$
The denominators are nonzero on the indicated patches, so both one-forms
are smooth there. Differentiation gives
$d[(1-\cos\theta)d\phi]=d[-(1+\cos\theta)d\phi]=\omega$ and
$d(-q_e r^{-1}dt)=-q_e r^{-2}dt\wedge dr$. Thus both potentials
differentiate to [F1]. Subtracting them gives
$\mathcal A_S-\mathcal A_N=-2q_m d\phi$ on the overlap.

If a global smooth one-form $\mathcal A$ with $d\mathcal A=\mathcal F$
existed and $q_m\ne0$, apply [F3] to the oriented sphere cycle $S_r$:
$$4\pi q_m=\int_{S_r}\mathcal F=\int_{S_r}d\mathcal A =\int_{\partial S_r}\mathcal A=0,$$
since $\partial S_r=0$. This contradiction rules out a global potential
when $q_m\ne0$.

If $q_m=0$, the one-form $\mathcal A=-q_e r^{-1}dt$ is smooth and
global on $\mathbb R_t\times J\times S^2$, and its exterior derivative is
$\mathcal F$. This proves the exact criterion.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters. Set
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$ and
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}.$$
The selected ingoing RN manifold is
$$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}:=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2,$$
where $v,r$ have units of metres, $S^2$ has unit round metric $\gamma$ and
outward area form $\omega$, and the signature is $(-,+,+,+)$. Orient the
product by $dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. Define
$$g_{\mathrm{in}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\gamma,\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dv\wedge dr+q_m\omega.$$
These are smooth on every $r>0$, including every positive root of $f$; the
domain excludes $r=0$. This is an extension of the static RN metric and field,
not a maximal extension or a specification of a source at the excluded
centre.

For the time orientation, define the global smooth fields
$$\ell:=-\partial_r,\qquad n:=\partial_v+\frac{f(r)}2\partial_r,\qquad N:=\ell+n=\partial_v+\left(\frac{f(r)}2-1\right)\partial_r.$$
The chosen future timelike field is $N$; the future cone is the component of
the timelike cone containing it. The well-definedness proof shows that $N$ is

A **Killing horizon for $\xi$** is a null hypersurface whose nonzero-generator part $H_*:=\{p\in H:\xi_p\ne0\}$ is nonempty and dense in $H$, and on that part the specified field is tangent, null and normal: $\xi_p\in T_pH$ and $g(\xi_p,X)=0$ for every $X\in T_pH$. A generator parameter or asymptotic normalization, when required, must be specified separately.

On $H_*$ the **signed surface gravity** for this precise $\xi$ is the unique smooth scalar $\kappa_H$ such that

$$d\bigl(g(\xi,\xi)\bigr)_p=-2\kappa_H(p)\,\xi^\flat_p\quad(p\in H_*).$$

This is an equality of ambient covectors at points of $H$, not merely of their pullbacks to $TH$. No constancy or positivity is asserted. Under a nonzero constant rescaling $\xi'=a\xi$, $\kappa'_H=a\kappa_H$. A **bifurcation surface** is a specified smooth spacelike two-surface $B$ where the extended Killing field vanishes and the specified horizon branches meet (or have $B$ as their common boundary). $$\operatorname{Area}_g(S):=\sup\left\{\int_S\chi\mu_h:\chi\in C_c^\infty(S),\ 0\le\chi\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

with the extended order of [[def-extended-reals]]. On compact $S$ this is $\int_S\mu_h$; orientation is unnecessary. The density glues by [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]]. $$\mathcal E_{U,r}:=\left\{p\in U:\exists\gamma\text{ admissible from }p\ \forall R>0\ \exists t\in[0,T):r(\gamma(t))>R\right\}.$$

The **selected escape boundary** is $\partial_U\mathcal E_{U,r}$. No geodesic restriction, conformal completion, event-horizon identification or maximal extension is implicit in this definition.

An **extension obstruction at that approach** means no such extension and added point can realize the stated approach. In particular, unbounded absolute values of a polynomial complete contraction of the curvature tensor and metric inverse along $x_n$ obstruct such an approached $C^2$ nondegenerate extension. This criterion concerns curvature without its covariant derivatives. A smooth metric extension is the same definition with smooth $\widetilde g$. These notions alone assert neither a distributional matter source nor geodesic incompleteness.

Relative to a future unit observer $n$, an electric or magnetic spatial covector is identified with a spatial vector only by raising with the positive rest metric $h=g+n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$ on $n^\perp$. function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,

primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false

In the ingoing chart the $v,r$ block is
$\begin{pmatrix}-f&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $-1$ for every
$r>0$. Its inverse is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&f\end{pmatrix}$, so the
block has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. The sphere block
$r^2\gamma$ is positive definite, and the two-form in [F1] is smooth.
Therefore every positive root is a regular crossing without using a static
coordinate at that root.

Assume $M^2>Q^2$. Put $s=\sqrt{M^2-Q^2}$. Since $Q^2>0$,
$s^2=M^2-Q^2<M^2$ and $s,M\ge0$, so $s<M$ and $r_-=M-s>0$. Set
$r_+=M+s$, $d=r_+-r_->0$, and $x=r-r_+$. Then
$$f(r)=\frac{(r-r_+)(r-r_-)}{r^2}=x b(r),\qquad b(r):=\frac{r-r_-}{r^2},\qquad 2\kappa=b(r_+)=\frac d{r_+^2}>0.$$
The explicit algebraic factorization
$$2\kappa-b(r)= \frac{(r-r_+)(d r-r_+r_-)}{r_+^2r^2}$$
shows that
$$p(r):=\frac1{f(r)}-\frac1{2\kappa(r-r_+)} =\frac{d r-r_+r_-}{2\kappa r_+^2(r-r_-)}$$
is smooth near $r_+$ after shrinking the interval so $r-r_-\ne0$.
Define $h(r):=\int_{r_+}^{r}p(s)\,ds$. By [F4], $h'=p$; repeated
differentiation of this identity shows $h$ is smooth, and $h(r_+)=0$.

Define
$$K(r):=\frac{r-r_+}{\ell_*}e^{2\kappa h(r)}.$$
It is smooth and $K'(r_+)=\ell_*^{-1}>0$. By [F3], it has a smooth local
inverse $r=\rho(z)$ near $z=0$. After shrinking again, $K'(r)>0$ and
$$\frac{f(r)K'(r)}{K(r)}=2\kappa\qquad(r\ne r_+),$$
which follows by differentiating $K$ and using the definition of $h$.
The identity extends in the equivalent form $fK'=2\kappa K$ to $r=r_+$.

For the original ingoing region define $V=e^{\kappa v}$ and
$U=-K(r)e^{-\kappa v}$. The Jacobian of $(v,r)\mapsto(U,V)$ is
$\kappa K'(r)>0$, so this is a smooth local coordinate change across the
future crossing. Since $UV=-K(r)$, the inverse radial coordinate is
$r=\rho(-UV)$. Differentiation gives
$$dv=\frac{dV}{\kappa V},\qquad dr=-\frac{V}{K'(r)}dU-\frac{U}{K'(r)}dV.$$
Substitute these in $-f\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr$; the $dV^2$ coefficient cancels
by $fK'=2\kappa K$ and $K=-UV$, leaving
$$-\frac1{\kappa K'(\rho(-UV))} (dU\otimes dV+dV\otimes dU).$$
This coefficient is smooth and nonzero at $U=V=0$. The sphere term
$\rho(-UV)^2\gamma$ is smooth and positive definite, so the radial block
retains Lorentz signature throughout a small rectangle. To make this a local
extension chart, choose $\varepsilon>0$ so $\rho(-UV)>0$ for
$(U,V)\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^2$. The original ingoing model maps
the open subset whose image satisfies $V>0$, $|U|,|V|<\varepsilon$ smoothly
and bijectively onto that open half-rectangle, by the nonzero Jacobian above.
Adjoin the full rectangle and identify that half with the old subset. A
sequence in the overlap tending inside the new rectangle but outside the
half-rectangle can only approach $V=0$; there $v=\kappa^{-1}\log V$
tends to $-\infty$, so it has no limit at any finite old point. The other
edges lie outside the open rectangle. Thus the local gluing separates the
new points from all old points, and the displayed coordinates and metric
give a smooth Hausdorff local extension.

The electric two-form transforms as
$$-\frac{q_e}{r^2}dv\wedge dr =-\frac{q_e}{\kappa r^2K'(r)}dU\wedge dV,$$
whose coefficient is smooth because $r_+>0$, $\kappa>0$, and $K'(r_+)>0$;
$q_m\omega$ is unchanged. Since
$dv\wedge dr=(\kappa K'(r))^{-1}dU\wedge dV$ with positive coefficient,
the product orientation extends as $dU\wedge dV\wedge\omega$.
Thus the two-form extends smoothly over both axes. The vector field transforms to
$$\partial_v=\kappa(V\partial_V-U\partial_U).$$
The extended metric coefficients depend only on $UV$, which is invariant
under this vector field; also $\mathcal L_{\partial_v}dU=-\kappa dU$ and
$\mathcal L_{\partial_v}dV=\kappa dV$, so the radial metric tensor is
invariant. By [F5] the extended field is Killing. It vanishes at $U=V=0$,
where the induced sphere metric is $r_+^2\gamma$. Each null axis is a smooth null hypersurface: on $U=0$ its generator has covector $-V/K'(r_+)\,dU$, and on $V=0$ it has covector $U/K'(r_+)\,dV$. Thus the Killing field is tangent, null and normal, nonzero away from the common sphere; that portion is nonempty and dense on each axis. The axes meet precisely at the spacelike sphere where the extended field vanishes.

On each quadrant $UV\ne0$, define
$$t:=\frac{1}{2\kappa}\log\left|\frac VU\right|,\qquad r=\rho(-UV).$$
These are smooth coordinates there: $r=\rho(-UV)$ and the logarithmic ratio
independently determine the product and quotient of the nonzero coordinates,
so their Jacobian is nonzero. Differentiating gives
$$dr=-\frac{V\,dU+U\,dV}{K'(r)},\qquad dt=\frac{1}{2\kappa}\left(\frac{dV}{V}-\frac{dU}{U}\right),\qquad dt\wedge dr=\frac{1}{\kappa K'(r)}dU\wedge dV.$$
Put $\alpha=dU/U$ and $\eta=dV/V$. Since $UV=-K(r)$, the displayed
differentials give $dr=(K/K')(\alpha+\eta)$ and
$dt=(\eta-\alpha)/(2\kappa)$. Substituting in the static radial metric
$-fdt^2+f^{-1}dr^2$ of [F1], and using $fK'=2\kappa K$ from step 2.1,
the $\alpha\otimes\alpha$ and $\eta\otimes\eta$ coefficients cancel
and each cross coefficient is $f/(2\kappa^2)=K/(\kappa K')$. Therefore
the radial tensor is
$$\frac{K}{\kappa K'}(\alpha\otimes\eta+\eta\otimes\alpha) =-\frac1{\kappa K'}(dU\otimes dV+dV\otimes dU),$$
using $K=-UV$. The sphere term remains $r^2\gamma$. The two-form satisfies
$-q_e r^{-2}dt\wedge dr+q_m\omega
=-q_e(\kappa r^2K')^{-1}dU\wedge dV+q_m\omega$, exactly its expression
from step 4.1. Thus each quadrant is a static RN chart with $f\ne0$.
Since $\kappa K'(r)>0$, its orientation agrees with
$dt\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. The exact static-domain interface [L1] makes
the geometric Einstein and Maxwell residuals vanish on all four quadrants.
The metric, field and inverse metric are smooth on the full extension chart,
so the residual tensors are continuous; a continuous tensor vanishing on a

Let $M,a,q\in\mathbb R$ have units of metres. Write
$$\Sigma(r,\theta):=r^2+a^2\cos^2\theta,\quad \Delta(r):=r^2-2Mr+a^2+q^2,\quad R(r):=r^2+a^2,\quad B(\theta):=\sin^2\theta.$$
Let $U$ be an open subset of the Boyer-Lindquist coordinate region
$\{(x^0,r,\theta,\phi):\Sigma>0,\ \Delta\ne0,\ 0<\theta<\pi\}$.
Coordinates $x^0,r$ have units of metres and $\theta,\phi$ are dimensionless.
On $U$ define
$$g=-\frac{\Delta}{\Sigma}(dx^0-aB\,d\phi)^2 +\frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}\,dr^2+\Sigma\,d\theta^2 +\frac{B}{\Sigma}(R\,d\phi-a\,dx^0)^2,\qquad \mathcal A=-\frac{qr}{\Sigma}(dx^0-aB\,d\phi),\quad\mathcal F:=d\mathcal A.$$
The metric is the exact real symmetric tensor given by this display; no value
on $\Delta=0$, the axes $\theta=0,\pi$, or $\Sigma=0$ is part of this
definition. The scalar $q$ is a geometric electric flux-length parameter; no
SI conversion is fixed in this Definition.

**Well-definedness on the stated patch.** In the coordinates
$(x^0,r,y,\phi)$ with $y=\cos\theta$ and $b=1-y^2$, the coordinate change is
a smooth diffeomorphism because $dy/d\theta=-\sin\theta\ne0$. The metric
matrix has
$$g_{00}=-\frac{\Delta-a^2b}{\Sigma},\quad g_{03}=-\frac{ab(R-\Delta)}{\Sigma},\quad g_{33}=\frac{b(R^2-a^2\Delta b)}{\Sigma},\quad g_{11}=\frac{\Sigma}{\Delta},\quad g_{22}=\frac{\Sigma}{b}.$$
The inverse has nonzero entries
$$g^{00}=-\frac{R^2-a^2\Delta b}{\Sigma\Delta},\quad g^{03}=-\frac{a(R-\Delta)}{\Sigma\Delta},\quad g^{33}=\frac{\Delta-a^2b}{\Sigma\Delta b},\quad g^{11}=\frac{\Delta}{\Sigma},\quad g^{22}=\frac{b}{\Sigma}.$$
Multiplying the $0,3$ blocks and the reciprocal $1,1$ and $2,2$ entries
gives $gg^{-1}=I_4$.
The $t,\phi$ block determinant is $-\Delta b$, and the full determinant is
$-\Sigma^2$ in these coordinates. If $\Delta>0$, the $t,\phi$ block has one
positive and one negative eigenvalue while the $r,\theta$ entries are positive.
If $\Delta<0$, $g_{33}>0$ and the $t,\phi$ block has positive determinant,
hence is positive definite, while $g_{11}<0$ and $g_{22}>0$. Thus $g$ is
nondegenerate of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on every component of $U$. Since this
is a coordinate patch, a smooth time orientation may be supplied locally;
the geometric electrovac equations below do not use its choice.

The potential is a smooth real one-form on $U$ because $\Sigma>0$, so $\mathcal F$
is a smooth real two-form. Exterior differentiation gives $d\mathcal F=d^2\mathcal A=0$
using commutation of smooth mixed coordinate derivatives. This definition is
only on the pole-free Boyer-Lindquist patch and asserts no global potential,
axis extension, horizon extension, or global topology.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $o$ is the manifold orientation, $N$ is a smooth future timelike field, and the metric volume form is chosen to agree with $o$. Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection, let $\mathcal F$ be a smooth real two-form on $M$, and use the curvature convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$.
Define
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where both raised indices use $g^{-1}$. A **geometric electrovac datum with zero cosmological constant** is the tuple $(M,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ satisfying
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$$
at every point of $M$. Here $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$; on two-forms $\star_g^2=-1$. No material current, matter tensor, global potential, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, horizon, or extension condition is part of this definition.

For an oriented embedded sphere $S$ on which the integrals converge, define its geometric electric and magnetic flux parameters by
$$q_e(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\star_g\mathcal F,\qquad q_m(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\mathcal F.$$
When $M$ and the coordinates have length units, these parameters have units of length. A magnetic flux need not have a global potential; no flux quantization is included. The background Lorentzian geometry and Hodge conventions carry the countable-choice assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of their named suppliers; the algebraic identities in this definition require no additional choice principle.

For $M,a,q\in\mathbb R$, on every pole-free Boyer-Lindquist domain with
$\Sigma>0$ and $\Delta\ne0$, the metric and potential of
[[def-emg-xs-kn-data]] satisfy the equations below. In addition, for every
$R_0>4|M|$, the full-sphere exterior extension of
[[def-emg-xs-kn-full-sphere-exterior]] satisfies the same equations on
$\mathbb R_{x^0}\times(R_0,\infty)\times S^2$. On all these domains,
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=2\left(\mathcal F_{ik}\mathcal F_j{}^k -\frac14g_{ij}\mathcal F_{kl}\mathcal F^{kl}\right).$$
Thus it is a geometric electrovac datum on every such chart component. No
maximal extension, uniqueness, horizon classification, or physical
measurement is asserted.

For arbitrary formal $c,\mu_0,G_N>0$, set $\alpha=\sqrt{4\pi G_N/(\mu_0c^4)}$, $F=\mathcal F/\alpha$, and $T_{ab}:=\mu_0^{-1}Q_g(F)_{ab}$. Then the same datum satisfies

$$dF=d(\star_gF)=0,\qquad S=0,\qquad G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}T_{ab},$$

where $S$ is scalar curvature and $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\frac12Sg_{ab}$. This is the formal SI-to-geometric tensor normalization of [[lem-emg-maxwell-observer-stress]](d). It asserts neither measured parameter values nor a bundle realization for arbitrary flux. When the separate fixed-sector action hypotheses hold, $T$ is also the electromagnetic Hilbert tensor of that supplier.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

$$\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle_g:=\det\bigl(g^{-1}(\alpha_i,\beta_j)\bigr),$$

and extend it bilinearly. For $0\le k\le4$, its coordinate expression is the pointwise exterior metric on $k$-covectors

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k}\beta^{a_1\cdots a_k},$$

where indices are raised by $g^{-1}$. There is a unique smooth bundle map $\star_g:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{4-k}(M)$ characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_g\,\mathrm{vol}_g$$

at every point. In a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, put $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, let $I^c$ be its increasing complement, let $s(I,I^c)$ be the sign of the permutation $(I,I^c)$ to $(0,1,2,3)$, and set $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$. Then

$$\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}.$$

Consequently, on $k$-forms,

$$\star_g^2=(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}\operatorname{id}.$$

In particular $\star_g^2=-\operatorname{id}$ on two-forms. For a two-form $F$, the component formula in a positively oriented chart is

$$({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}.$$

The exterior derivative in [[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]] has the local coordinate formula of [[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]], satisfies $d^2=0$, and obeys the graded product rule of [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-is-a-graded-derivation]].

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$g_p^{-1}$ and $g^{ab}$ be the inverse metric and its chart components as in
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]. Then:

1. For every smooth chart $(U,x)$ the component functions $g^{ab}:U\to\mathbb R$
   are $C^\infty$ on $U$.
2. For overlapping smooth charts $(U,x)$, $(V,y)$ the components satisfy the
   contravariant transformation law

$$g'^{ab}(u)=\sum_{c,d=0}^{3}\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^c}\bigl(x(u)\bigr)\, \frac{\partial y^b}{\partial x^d}\bigl(x(u)\bigr)\,g^{cd}\bigl(x(u)\bigr),\qquad u\in y(U\cap V),$$

where every component evaluated at a coordinate tuple is its coordinate
representative, as in [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
$x(u)$ denotes $(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$, and $\partial y^a/\partial x^c$ are
the entries of $D(y\circ x^{-1})$.

3. Consequently the pointwise bilinear forms $g_p^{-1}$ on $T_p^*M$ are
   presented by component functions that are smooth in every chart and glue by
   the contravariant law; the inverse metric is a well-defined smooth component
   family determined by $g$ alone.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

The sphere coordinates $X,Y,Z$ and one-form $\beta=X\,dY-Y\,dX$ are
smooth globally. Since $r>0$, $\Sigma=r^2+a^2Z^2>0$; every coefficient in
the displayed product tensors is therefore smooth, and $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}$
is smooth by exterior differentiation. In polar charts,
$\beta=\sin^2\theta\,d\psi$ and
$\gamma=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\psi^2$.

Away from the axes and roots, put $\beta=\sin^2\theta\,d\psi$ and
set $$dv=dx^0+\frac R\Delta dr,\qquad d\psi=d\phi+\frac a\Delta dr.$$
This triangular coordinate change has Jacobian determinant $1$. Substitution
in the product metric gives exactly the BL metric in [F1]. Also
$$dv-a\sin^2\theta\,d\psi=dx^0-a\sin^2\theta\,d\phi+\frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}dr.$$
Thus $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}}$ differs from the BL potential by the radial
one-form $-qr\Delta^{-1}dr$, whose exterior derivative is zero because its
coefficient depends only on $r$. The two field strengths agree. Finally
$dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega=dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega$, so this change
preserves the stated orientation.

On $0<\theta<\pi$, the determinant in coordinates
$(v,r,\theta,\psi)$ is $-\Sigma^2\sin^2\theta$: it is the determinant
$-\Sigma^2$ from [F1], multiplied by $(dy/d\theta)^2=\sin^2\theta$; the
coordinate change in step 1.2 has Jacobian $1$. This determinant is
nonzero when $\Delta\ne0$ and extends by continuity to $\Delta=0$, since
the product metric coefficients are smooth by step 1.1. At a polar axis
$\beta=0$ as a covector on the sphere tangent space; the radial block is
$\begin{pmatrix}-f_0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $-1$, and the
angular block is $\Sigma\gamma$, positive definite. So the metric is
nondegenerate at the axes too. On a large-$r$ pole-free region it has
signature $(-,+,+,+)$ by [F1] and step 1.2. A continuous nondegenerate
symmetric form has locally constant signature; the product manifold is
connected, so this signature holds everywhere.

The field $N$ is smooth and global by the product construction. Direct
contraction gives
$$g_{\mathrm{in}}(N,N)=-(f_0^2+f_0+1)=-\left((f_0+\tfrac12)^2+\tfrac34\right)<0.$$
Thus $N$ is everywhere timelike, and by [F6] it selects the stated smooth
time orientation on the whole product.

By [F3] the Einstein and Maxwell residual tensors vanish on the
pole-free BL domains. The coordinate and field identities in step 1.2 carry
that zero residual to the ingoing formulas on the dense set
$\Delta\ne0$, $0<\theta<\pi$. By steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1, the metric and
field are smooth and nondegenerate on the full product; [F4-F5] therefore
make each residual tensor continuous, including at the axes and roots. A
continuous tensor zero on a dense subset is zero on its closure. This proves
the stated conditional equation continuation exactly when the interface [F3]
is established, without extending beyond the selected ingoing model.

metric $\gamma$ and outward area form $\omega$. Define the global one-form
$\beta:=X\,dY-Y\,dX$ and the product
$$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}:=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2,$$
oriented by $dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. On this product define
$$\begin{aligned}g_{\mathrm{in}}={}&-\left(1-\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}\right)dv^2+2\,dv\,dr-2a\,dr\,\beta-2a\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}dv\odot\beta+\Sigma\gamma+a^2\left(1+\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}\right)\beta^2,\\\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}}={}&-\frac{qr}{\Sigma}(dv-a\beta),\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}:=d\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}},\end{aligned}$$
where $u\odot w=(u\otimes w+w\otimes u)/2$. The time-orientation field

sphere for every $r>0$, including each positive root of $\Delta$; no

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters. Set
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$ and
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}.$$
The selected ingoing RN manifold is
$$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}:=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2,$$
where $v,r$ have units of metres, $S^2$ has unit round metric $\gamma$ and
outward area form $\omega$, and the signature is $(-,+,+,+)$. Orient the
product by $dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. Define
$$g_{\mathrm{in}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\gamma,\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dv\wedge dr+q_m\omega.$$
These are smooth on every $r>0$, including every positive root of $f$; the
domain excludes $r=0$. This is an extension of the static RN metric and field,
not a maximal extension or a specification of a source at the excluded
centre.

For the time orientation, define the global smooth fields
$$\ell:=-\partial_r,\qquad n:=\partial_v+\frac{f(r)}2\partial_r,\qquad N:=\ell+n=\partial_v+\left(\frac{f(r)}2-1\right)\partial_r.$$
The chosen future timelike field is $N$; the future cone is the component of
the timelike cone containing it. The well-definedness proof shows that $N$ is
timelike and that $\ell,n$ are future null. On $f\ne0$, the substitution
$v=t+r_*(r)$ with $r_*'=1/f$ identifies the metric and two-form with the
static dyonic RN formulas of [[def-emg-xs-rn-data]]. This coordinate
identification does not assert agreement of time orientations on the
interior static components: on $f>0$ the selected orientation agrees with
$\partial_t$, while on $f<0$ it is the opposite of the separate choice
$\partial_r$ made by that static definition.

Let $M,a,q\in\mathbb R$ have units of metres. Set
$$\Sigma=r^2+a^2\cos^2\theta,\quad \Delta=r^2-2Mr+a^2+q^2,\quad R=r^2+a^2,$$
and let $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ have unit round
metric $\gamma$ and outward area form $\omega$. Define the global one-form
$\beta:=X\,dY-Y\,dX$ and the product
$$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}:=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2,$$
oriented by $dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. On this product define
$$\begin{aligned}g_{\mathrm{in}}={}&-\left(1-\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}\right)dv^2+2\,dv\,dr-2a\,dr\,\beta-2a\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}dv\odot\beta+\Sigma\gamma+a^2\left(1+\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma}\right)\beta^2,\\\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}}={}&-\frac{qr}{\Sigma}(dv-a\beta),\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}:=d\mathcal A_{\mathrm{in}},\end{aligned}$$
where $u\odot w=(u\otimes w+w\otimes u)/2$. The time-orientation field
is $$f_0:=1-\frac{2Mr-q^2}{\Sigma},\qquad N:=\partial_v-\frac{1+f_0^2}{2}\partial_r.$$
These formulas define smooth Lorentzian metric and field data on the whole
sphere for every $r>0$, including each positive root of $\Delta$; no
maximal extension, $r=0$ locus, or global uniqueness is asserted. On the
dense pole-free set where $\Delta\ne0$, they are related to the
Boyer-Lindquist data by the advanced coordinate change proved below.

The source-free geometric electrovac equations extend across $\Delta=0$
conditionally on the exact current interface of

on the dense complement of the roots and axes, and smoothness then extends

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

$\gamma(t)\in V$ one has $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V$. Thus no causal curve can
leave $V$ and later re-enter it; a set $V$ with this property for all causal
curves is called **causally convex for causal curves that meet it twice**.

**(c) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is **globally hyperbolic** when it is
strongly causal and for all $p,q\in M$ the **causal diamond**
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact in the subspace topology
([[def-compact-space]]).

**(d) Time functions.** A **time function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a function
$u:M\to\mathbb R$ which is continuous from the manifold topology to the usual topology of
$\mathbb R$: for every $p\in M$ and every open neighborhood $W$ of $u(p)$
there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $u(V)\subseteq W$
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). It also satisfies
$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ that is not constant on $[a,b]$.

**(e) Temporal functions.** A **temporal function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
function $u:M\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]])
whose gradient is past-directed timelike: writing $du$ for its differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]) and $\nabla u$ for the vector field
with $g(\nabla u,X)=du(X)$ for every smooth vector field $X$, constructed from
the inverse metric of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], one
has
$$g(\nabla u,\nabla u)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad du(N)=g(\nabla u,N)>0 .$$
The first inequality says that the gradient is nowhere zero and timelike; the
second fixes it as past-directed for the chosen time orientation. No level set
of a temporal function is asserted here to be a hypersurface or to be
spacelike, and no relation between temporal functions and compactness is
asserted; those claims are proved separately where they are used.

**(f) Scope and conventions.** These are mathematical conditions on the
Lorentzian model. Different sources define global hyperbolicity by equivalent
but differently phrased conditions; this page fixes the formulation of (c)
and proves the implications it uses. In particular no equivalence between
global hyperbolicity and the existence of a Cauchy hypersurface is asserted
by this definition, and the physical reading of strong causality or global
hyperbolicity as predictability of a classical model is adopted only in the
framework postulates.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Write
$N_p^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,N_p)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and let $T_p$ be the
timelike set, with components $C_p^+$ (the one containing $N_p$) and $C_p^-$,
and with future and past causality as fixed in
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] and
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Then:

1. $N_p^{\perp}$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $T_pM$, and $g_p$ is
   positive definite on it; equivalently, every nonzero $v\in T_pM$ with
   $g_p(v,N_p)=0$ is spacelike.
2. $g_p(v,N_p)\neq0$ for every nonzero causal $v\in T_pM$.
3. $C_p^+=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)<0\}$, and
   $C_p^-=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\text{ and }g_p(v,N_p)>0\}$.
4. A nonzero $v\in T_pM$ is causal and future-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)$, and causal and past-directed if and only if
   $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)$. Consequently
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the set of
   future-directed causal vectors and $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)\setminus\{0\}$
   exactly the set of past-directed causal vectors,
   $\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C_p^-)=\{0\}$, and every
   nonzero causal vector is exactly one of future-directed and past-directed.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Then there is an open
neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ of $p$ and a smooth future-directed tetrad field
$(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$
([[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]), i.e.
$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$ for all $q\in U$ with
$E_0(q)$ future-directed for every $q\in U$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $a>0$, integer $m$ and integer $n\ge1$, define the rational regime by

$$
a^{m/n}:=(a^{1/n})^m,
$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique positive root of $s^n=a$ in [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], and integer powers include reciprocals for negative $m$. This is [[def-rational-power]]; [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]] proves independence of the fraction representative and [[lem-rational-power-laws]] gives the rational exponent laws. The supplementary convention is $0^r=0$ for rational $r>0$; $0^0$ and negative powers of zero remain undefined.

The separate real regime is [[def-real-power]]: for $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, $a^x=\exp(x\log a)$, with the laws of [[thm-real-power-laws]]. For $x>0$ set $0^x=0$; no arbitrary real power is assigned to a negative base. The real-power laws are supplied by that theorem, not inferred from the rational root formula. Use the real-number structure of [[def-real-numbers]].

In particular $s(q)=q^{1/2}$ for $q>0$ is the unique positive solution of $s(q)^2=q$. Its smoothness and derivative are a separate well-definedness result, not an assumption about fractional notation.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim:
In RN, $d\tau=dv-dr$ and the inverse $v,r$ block of [F1] gives
$$g^{-1}(d\tau,d\tau)=f-2,$$
which equals $-2$ at $r_H$. After shrinking a radial collar it remains
negative, and $d\tau(N)=2-f/2>0$. In KN, direct inversion of [F2] gives
$$g^{-1}(d\tau,d\tau) =\frac{a^2\sin^2\theta-2R+\Delta}{\Sigma}.$$
At $r_H$, $\Delta=0$, $R=r_H^2+a^2$, and the numerator satisfies
$a^2\sin^2\theta-2R\le-2r_H^2-a^2<0$. Compactness of $S^2$ and
continuity therefore give a uniform radial collar where this norm stays
negative. There $d\tau(N)=1+(1+f_0^2)/2>0$. Thus $\nabla\tau$ is past
timelike in either case by [F3-F4]. In a local future orthonormal tetrad,
write $-\nabla\tau=(T^0,\mathbf T)$ and a future causal
$Z=(Z^0,\mathbf Z)$. Then $T^0>\|\mathbf T\|$ and
$Z^0\ge\|\mathbf Z\|$, with $Z^0>0$, by the signature and selected cone.
By [F9],
$$g(-\nabla\tau,Z)=-T^0Z^0+\mathbf T\cdot\mathbf Z \le-(T^0-\|\mathbf T\|)Z^0<0.$$
Therefore $d\tau(Z)=g(\nabla\tau,Z)>0$.

At an RN root, $\xi=\partial_v$ satisfies
$\xi^\flat=-f\,dv+dr=dr$, and $g(\xi,N)=-1<0$ there, so it is future
null by [F5]. At a KN root put $R_H=r_H^2+a^2$ and
$$\chi=\partial_v+\frac{a}{R_H}\Psi.$$
Substitution in the metric of [F2] gives
$\chi^\flat=(\Sigma_H/R_H)dr$, where
$\Sigma_H=r_H^2+a^2\cos^2\theta>0$. Also
$dr(N)=-(1+f_0^2)/2<0$, so
$g(\chi,N)=\chi^\flat(N)<0$ and $\chi$ is future null. In both cases
$dr$ on the root is a positive multiple of the covector of a future null
generator. In an orthonormal frame, if future null $K=(K^0,\mathbf K)$ and
future causal $Z=(Z^0,\mathbf Z)$, then $K^0=\|\mathbf K\|$,
$Z^0\ge\|\mathbf Z\|$, and
$$g(K,Z)=-K^0Z^0+\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf Z \le-K^0Z^0+\|\mathbf K\|\|\mathbf Z\|\le0.$$
Consequently $dr(Z)\le0$ on $r=r_H$.

Put $u:=-g^{-1}(d\tau,d\tau)>0$ on the collar by step 1.1.
The unique positive root $\sqrt u$ is smooth: at every $u_0>0$ the map
$s\mapsto s^2$ has derivative $2\sqrt{u_0}\ne0$, so [F7] gives a smooth
local inverse; uniqueness makes these local inverses agree. Hence
$n_\tau:=-\nabla\tau/\sqrt u$ is a smooth future unit timelike field.
At $v=0$, cover the compact sphere section at $r=r_H$ by finitely many
relatively compact neighborhoods on which [F6] supplies smooth future
orthonormal tetrads $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$. Shrink $\delta$ so the closed radial
collar over each smaller patch stays in its tetrad neighborhood. Extend
these tetrads to all $v$ by the isometric translations of [F1-F2]; both
metrics and $d\tau$ are $v$-translation invariant. On each neighborhood set
$P_i:=E_i+g(E_i,n_\tau)n_\tau$ for $i=1,2,3$. Then $d\tau(P_i)=0$. If
$\sum_i c_iP_i=0$, then $\sum_i c_iE_i$ is a multiple of $n_\tau$; its
squared norm is nonnegative, while a nonzero multiple of $n_\tau$ has
negative squared norm. Hence all $c_i=0$. The kernel of $d\tau$ is positive
definite, so finite Gram-Schmidt gives a smooth orthonormal screen
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ after shrinking each neighborhood. Its normalization roots
are smooth by the same inverse argument. Every future causal vector with
$d\tau(Z)=1$ has
$$Z=\frac{n_\tau+b_1e_1+b_2e_2+b_3e_3}{d\tau(n_\tau)},\qquad b_1^2+b_2^2+b_3^2\le1.$$
Indeed, write $Z=s n_\tau+W$ with $W\perp n_\tau$. Since $n_\tau$ is future
timelike and $Z$ is future causal, [F5] gives $g(n_\tau,Z)<0$, so
$s=-g(n_\tau,Z)>0$. Causality gives $g(W,W)\le s^2$, and
$d\tau(Z)=s\sqrt u=1$.

On each finite coordinate patch of step 2.1, the function
$G(r,\omega,b):=dr(Z)$ for the displayed normalized vector is smooth in
the radial variable, the compact sphere-coordinate subset and the closed
unit ball $b\in\mathbb R^3$. Their products with the closed radial interval
and unit ball are closed bounded Euclidean sets, hence compact by [F8].
Applying the extreme-value theorem [F8] to $|\partial_rG|$ on each product
and taking the largest of finitely many bounds gives one finite $C\ge0$,
uniform in $v$. At $r=r_H$, step 1.2 gives
$G(r_H,\omega,b)\le0$. The one-variable mean-value theorem [F10] therefore
gives, throughout the collar,
$$G(r,\omega,b)\le G(r_H,\omega,b)+C|r-r_H| \le C|r-r_H|.$$
For any nonzero future causal $Z$, step 1.1 gives $d\tau(Z)>0$; apply the
normalized estimate to $Z/d\tau(Z)$ and multiply back. The zero vector is
trivial. This proves the asserted cone bound including all angular screen
directions.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters. Set
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$ and
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}.$$
The selected ingoing RN manifold is
$$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}:=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2,$$
where $v,r$ have units of metres, $S^2$ has unit round metric $\gamma$ and
outward area form $\omega$, and the signature is $(-,+,+,+)$. Orient the
product by $dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega$. Define
$$g_{\mathrm{in}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\gamma,\qquad \mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dv\wedge dr+q_m\omega.$$
These are smooth on every $r>0$, including every positive root of $f$; the
domain excludes $r=0$. This is an extension of the static RN metric and field,
not a maximal extension or a specification of a source at the excluded
centre.

For the time orientation, define the global smooth fields
$$\ell:=-\partial_r,\qquad n:=\partial_v+\frac{f(r)}2\partial_r,\qquad N:=\ell+n=\partial_v+\left(\frac{f(r)}2-1\right)\partial_r.$$
The chosen future timelike field is $N$; the future cone is the component of
the timelike cone containing it. The well-definedness proof shows that $N$ is
timelike and that $\ell,n$ are future null. On $f\ne0$, the substitution
$v=t+r_*(r)$ with $r_*'=1/f$ identifies the metric and two-form with the
static dyonic RN formulas of [[def-emg-xs-rn-data]]. This coordinate
identification does not assert agreement of time orientations on the
interior static components: on $f>0$ the selected orientation agrees with
$\partial_t$, while on $f<0$ it is the opposite of the separate choice
$\partial_r$ made by that static definition.

Consider either (i) the selected ingoing RN model with $M>0$, $Q^2>0$,
$M^2\ge Q^2$, and
$r_H=M+\sqrt{M^2-Q^2}$, or (ii) the selected ingoing KN model with $M>0$,
$M^2\ge a^2+q^2>0$, and
$r_H=M+\sqrt{M^2-a^2-q^2}$. In each case $r_H>0$. There is
$\delta>0$ and a collar
$$\mathcal C=\mathbb R_v\times(r_H-\delta,r_H+\delta)\times S^2$$
on which $\tau:=v-r$ is a smooth temporal function in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]: its gradient is past
timelike and $d\tau(Z)>0$ for every nonzero future causal vector $Z$. There
is a finite $C\ge0$ such that
$$dr(Z)\le C|r-r_H|\,d\tau(Z)$$
for every future causal $Z$ over the collar. On $r=r_H$ one also has
$dr(Z)\le0$. This is a local cone estimate on the two specified metrics; it
is not an event-horizon theorem.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable boundaryless four-manifold with smooth Lorentz metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time orientation. All definitions below are mathematical. A solution of a specified covariant field system is a tuple of fields of the regularity stated by that system satisfying its equations on its stated domain; this terminology alone supplies neither existence nor a global electromagnetic potential.

**(a) Global causal and Cauchy conventions.** Use exactly [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]: a future causal curve is locally absolutely continuous in coordinate charts, has nonzero future causal derivative almost everywhere, and has no constant subinterval. Inextendibility and causal reachability $J^\pm$ have that item's endpoint-extension meanings. A Cauchy set meets every inextendible causal curve at exactly one parameter value: its inverse image under each such curve is a singleton, as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]. A spacelike hypersurface is a smooth embedded codimension-one submanifold with positive-definite induced metric; this local condition does not assert the global Cauchy property. Strong causality has the small-neighborhood no-leaving-and-reentering meaning of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]. Global hyperbolicity means strong causality and compactness of every $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$, exactly as there; no equivalence theorem is added here.

**(b) Null and Killing horizons.** A smooth embedded hypersurface $H\subset M$ is **null** when $g|_{TH}$ is degenerate. Equivalently, for any local defining function $f$ with $H=\{f=0\}$ and $df\ne0$ on $H$, $g^{-1}(df,df)=0$ on $H$. A specified smooth vector field $\xi$ is **Killing** when $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$, equivalently $\nabla_{(a}\xi_{b)}=0$, using [[def-gr-killing-field]] and [[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]]. A **Killing horizon for $\xi$** is a null hypersurface whose nonzero-generator part $H_*:=\{p\in H:\xi_p\ne0\}$ is nonempty and dense in $H$, and on that part the specified field is tangent, null and normal: $\xi_p\in T_pH$ and $g(\xi_p,X)=0$ for every $X\in T_pH$. A generator parameter or asymptotic normalization, when required, must be specified separately.

On $H_*$ the **signed surface gravity** for this precise $\xi$ is the unique smooth scalar $\kappa_H$ such that

$$d\bigl(g(\xi,\xi)\bigr)_p=-2\kappa_H(p)\,\xi^\flat_p\quad(p\in H_*).$$

This is an equality of ambient covectors at points of $H$, not merely of their pullbacks to $TH$. No constancy or positivity is asserted. Under a nonzero constant rescaling $\xi'=a\xi$, $\kappa'_H=a\kappa_H$. A **bifurcation surface** is a specified smooth spacelike two-surface $B$ where the extended Killing field vanishes and the specified horizon branches meet (or have $B$ as their common boundary). Surface gravity at such a surface means a smooth extension of the scalar from the adjacent nonzero-generator portions, with each point in their closure, only if that extension exists; the defining equation at $\xi=0$ alone determines no value. Neither a bifurcation surface nor such an extension is asserted to exist.

**(c) Sections, area and ergoregions.** A **horizon section** is a specified smooth spacelike embedded two-surface $S$ in the horizon, with positive induced metric $h$. Its area density is $\mu_h=\sqrt{\det(h_{ij})}\,|dy^1dy^2|$ of [[def-riemannian-volume-density]]. Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for intrinsic density integration, as in [[def-riemannian-volume-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]. Its possibly infinite area is the nonnegative extended value

$$\operatorname{Area}_g(S):=\sup\left\{\int_S\chi\mu_h:\chi\in C_c^\infty(S),\ 0\le\chi\le1\right\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

with the extended order of [[def-extended-reals]]. On compact $S$ this is $\int_S\mu_h$; orientation is unnecessary. The density glues by [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]]. A stationary field here is a specified Killing field timelike on a specified nonempty open region; no normalization is inferred from this adjective. ([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is

function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what

is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,

primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$
